subject: science
title: KS3 Science Reading — Chemistry: Chemical Reactions
subtitle: Reading practice on reactions, pH, neutralisation, combustion, displacement, and metals with acids.
description: A KS3 reading pack for chemical reactions. Passages use source-grounded explanations and questions that test retrieval, inference, explanation, and practical reasoning.

data.sourcePassage: A chemical reaction is a change in which new substances are formed. The starting substances are called reactants and the new substances are called products. During a reaction, atoms are rearranged into different combinations; they are not destroyed. Evidence such as fizzing, a colour change, a temperature change, light, or a new solid can suggest a reaction, but one observation alone is not always proof. For example, bubbles in a fizzy drink may simply be dissolved carbon dioxide escaping. Scientists compare observations with explanations, use controls, and repeat results. A word equation summarises a reaction using substance names. In magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide, the reactants are magnesium and oxygen, and the product is magnesium oxide.

questions.question: What are the starting substances in a chemical reaction called?
questions.modelAnswer: They are called reactants.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a chemical reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: A new substance is formed.

questions.question: Why do bubbles alone not always prove that a chemical reaction has happened?
questions.modelAnswer: Bubbles can also happen when dissolved gas escapes, such as carbon dioxide from a fizzy drink, so further evidence is needed.

questions.question: In the word equation magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide, name the product.
questions.modelAnswer: The product is magnesium oxide.

questions.question: Explain the difference between an observation and an explanation using fizzing as your example.
questions.modelAnswer: Fizzing is an observation because it is noticed directly. Saying that a gas is being produced is an explanation because it gives the scientific reason.

data.sourcePassage: The pH scale shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is. Acids have pH values below 7, neutral solutions have pH 7, and alkalis have pH values above 7. Universal indicator is useful because it gives a range of colours: red, orange, or yellow in acids; green near neutral; and blue or purple in alkalis. Litmus is simpler because it mainly shows acid or alkali. Blue litmus turns red in acid, while red litmus turns blue in alkali. Neutralisation happens when an acid reacts with a base or alkali. The usual KS3 word equation is acid + alkali -> salt + water. A mixture only reaches pH 7 if the correct amounts of acid and alkali react. If extra alkali is added, the mixture becomes alkaline again.

questions.question: What pH value is neutral?
questions.modelAnswer: pH 7 is neutral.

questions.question: Which colour is universal indicator near neutral?
questions.modelAnswer: Green.

questions.question: What are the products of acid + alkali?
questions.modelAnswer: The products are a salt and water.

questions.question: Why is universal indicator more useful than litmus for estimating pH?
questions.modelAnswer: Universal indicator gives a range of colours across the pH scale, while litmus mainly shows whether a solution is acidic or alkaline.

questions.question: Why might a neutralisation mixture become alkaline after it was green?
questions.modelAnswer: If more alkali is added after the correct amount, excess alkali remains and the pH rises above 7.

data.sourcePassage: Combustion means burning. It is usually a reaction with oxygen that releases energy as heat and often light. Combustion needs fuel, oxygen, and heat; these three requirements are called the fire triangle. Removing one part can stop a fire. A lid can reduce oxygen supply to a small flame, and water can cool some fires by removing heat. In a candle, wax is the fuel and oxygen comes from the air. Complete combustion of hydrocarbon fuels produces carbon dioxide and water. If there is not enough oxygen, incomplete combustion can happen. This may produce carbon monoxide and soot. Carbon monoxide is poisonous, so fuel-burning appliances need good ventilation and maintenance. Magnesium burning in oxygen makes a bright white flame and forms magnesium oxide.

questions.question: Name the three parts of the fire triangle.
questions.modelAnswer: Fuel, oxygen, and heat.

questions.question: What are the products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel?
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide and water.

questions.question: Why can putting a lid over a small flame put it out?
questions.modelAnswer: The lid reduces the oxygen supply, so one part of the fire triangle is removed.

questions.question: What white product forms when magnesium burns in oxygen?
questions.modelAnswer: Magnesium oxide forms.

questions.question: Explain why incomplete combustion is a safety concern.
questions.modelAnswer: Incomplete combustion can produce carbon monoxide, which is poisonous and difficult to detect without an alarm.

data.sourcePassage: A displacement reaction happens when a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound. At KS3, many examples use metals and metal salt solutions. A useful order is magnesium > zinc > iron > copper > silver. Zinc is more reactive than copper, so zinc can displace copper from copper sulfate solution. The word equation is zinc + copper sulfate -> zinc sulfate + copper. Observations may include the blue solution becoming paler and a copper-coloured coating forming on the zinc. Copper placed in zinc sulfate does not react because copper is less reactive than zinc. No visible change can be a useful result if it matches the prediction; it does not automatically mean the experiment failed.

questions.question: In the series magnesium > zinc > iron > copper > silver, which listed metal is most reactive?
questions.modelAnswer: Magnesium is the most reactive metal listed.

questions.question: Why can zinc displace copper from copper sulfate?
options: Zinc is less reactive than copper
Zinc is more reactive than copper
questions.modelAnswer: Zinc is more reactive than copper.

questions.question: Write the word equation for zinc reacting with copper sulfate.
questions.modelAnswer: zinc + copper sulfate -> zinc sulfate + copper.

questions.question: What observations might show that copper metal has formed?
questions.modelAnswer: A copper-coloured coating or solid appears, and the blue copper sulfate solution may become paler.

questions.question: Why is no visible change sometimes a valid result in a displacement test?
questions.modelAnswer: If the added metal is less reactive than the metal in the compound, no displacement is predicted, so no visible change supports the prediction.

data.section: Metals with acids and practical skills
data.sourcePassage: Many metals react with dilute acids to make a salt and hydrogen gas. The general word equation is metal + acid -> salt + hydrogen. With hydrochloric acid, magnesium makes magnesium chloride and hydrogen, zinc makes zinc chloride and hydrogen, and iron makes iron chloride and hydrogen. Copper does not usually react noticeably with dilute hydrochloric acid in KS3 classroom conditions because it is less reactive. To compare metals fairly, the type of metal is the independent variable. The dependent variable could be the time taken to collect 20 cm3 of hydrogen. Control variables include acid volume, acid concentration, metal mass, surface area, temperature, and apparatus. Repeats help spot anomalies and improve reliability. Hydrogen can be tested with a lit splint, which gives a squeaky pop, under teacher supervision.

questions.question: What gas is produced when many metals react with dilute acids?
questions.modelAnswer: Hydrogen is produced.

questions.question: What is the general word equation for many metals reacting with acids?
options: zinc + copper sulfate -> zinc sulfate + copper
questions.modelAnswer: metal + acid -> salt + hydrogen.

questions.question: Why is copper expected to show little or no reaction with dilute hydrochloric acid at KS3 level?
questions.modelAnswer: Copper is less reactive than metals such as magnesium, zinc, and iron, so it does not react noticeably in normal classroom conditions.

questions.question: Name two control variables for comparing metals with acid.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include acid volume, acid concentration, metal mass, metal surface area, temperature, and the same apparatus.

questions.question: Explain why repeats improve the reliability of reaction-rate results.
questions.modelAnswer: Repeats show whether results are consistent and help identify anomalies before drawing a conclusion.
